s025.description:
Task scam explained: the "get paid to like videos" job that ends with you paying them.
How app-optimisation and product-boosting job scams work, and the one rule that beats them.

It starts with an unexpected text or WhatsApp message. You like videos or rate products in sets of 40, an app shows your earnings climbing, and small early payouts make it feel real. Then a "double task" asks you to deposit your own money, usually in crypto, to unlock your earnings. The balance was never real. The FTC counted about 5,000 task-scam reports in all of 2023 and about 20,000 in just the first half of 2024. BBB Scam Tracker puts the median task-scam loss in 2025 at about $2,300. The FTC's rule: never pay to get paid.

Sources:
https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2024/12/new-ftc-data-show-skyrocketing-consumer-reports-about-game-online-job-scams
https://ftc.gov/system/files/ftc_gov/pdf/task-scams-spotlight-2024.pdf

s026.description:
Free trial auto-renew: why a "free" trial needs your card, and how companies profit when you forget to cancel.
Subscription traps, hard-to-find cancel buttons, and the Amazon Prime "Iliad" case.

When a free trial ends, the card on file is charged and the plan renews automatically. The US Federal Trade Commission accused Amazon of enrolling people in Prime without clear consent and making cancellation hard; internally the cancel flow was nicknamed "Iliad". Amazon denied wrongdoing but in September 2025 agreed to pay $2.5 billion to settle — a $1 billion civil penalty and $1.5 billion in customer refunds. The fix: set a reminder the day you sign up, and check your statement for charges you don't recognise. Not financial advice.

Sources:
https://www.click2houston.com/business/2025/09/25/amazon-to-pay-25-billion-to-settle-ftc-allegations-it-duped-customers-into-enrolling-in-prime/

s027.description:
Dynamic pricing explained: why the same eggs in the same store can show five different prices.
Personalised and algorithmic pricing: Instacart's price tests and AI airline fares.

Consumer Reports, Groundwork Collaborative and More Perfect Union found that Instacart showed nearly three in four grocery items at more than one price in an experiment; a dozen Lucerne eggs from one Safeway in Washington, D.C. showed $3.99, $4.28, $4.59, $4.69 or $4.79. Instacart ended its item price tests on 22 Dec 2025. Delta has said AI helps set fares on about 3% of its domestic flights, with plans for up to 20%; Delta says it doesn't target individuals with personalised fares. Before a big purchase, compare the price on another app, device or in the store.

Sources:
https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/instacart-ends-program-where-users-see-different-prices-for-the-same-item-at-same-store
